subtopic_title: Bisection of a given line segment.

record_links.rationale: This record explains line segment, bisect, and bisector.

record.evidence_quote: A line segment is part of a straight line. A line segment has a beginning and an end. When we are asked to **bisect** a line segment, we are asked to divide the line segment into two equal parts. The **bisector** is the line segment that divides the given line segment into two equal parts.
record.content_text:
A line segment is part of a straight line. A line segment has a beginning and an end. When we are asked to **bisect** a line segment, we are asked to divide the line segment into two equal parts.

The **bisector** is the line segment that divides the given line segment into two equal parts.

record_links.rationale: This record defines bisect and bisector.

record.evidence_quote: **bisect** When we bisect a line segment or an angle, we divide the line segment or the angle exactly in half. **bisector** A bisector is the line segment that divides the given line segment into two equal parts.
record.content_text:
**bisect** When we bisect a line segment or an angle, we divide the line segment or the angle exactly in half.

**bisector** A bisector is the line segment that divides the given line segment into two equal parts.

record_links.rationale: This worked example gives the straightedge-and-compass procedure for bisecting a line segment.

heading_path.h3: Worked example 14.4: Bisecting a line segment

record.evidence_quote: You are given line segment $AB$ as shown in the diagram below. Source image reference: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-14-049.png Bisect $AB$ and label the bisector $PQ$.
record.prompt_text:
You are given line segment $AB$ as shown in the diagram below.

Source image reference: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-14-049.png

Bisect $AB$ and label the bisector $PQ$.
record.answer_text:
Step 1: Draw the first set of two arcs.

Open the compass so that the distance between the two points is more than half of the length of $AB$. Test this on line $AB$.

Put the compass on point $A$ (the blue dot) and draw two arcs as shown. One arc is above $AB$ and one arc is below $AB$.

Source image reference: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-14-050.png

Step 2: Draw the second set of two arcs.

Keep the compass open at exactly the same width as for Step 1.

Put the compass on point $B$ (the orange dot) and draw two arcs as shown. One arc is above $AB$ and one arc is below $AB$.

Source image reference: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-14-051.png

Step 3: Draw the bisector.

Label the points where the arcs intersect as point $P$ and point $Q$.

Use a ruler and draw a line through point $P$ and point $Q$. $PQ$ is the bisector of line segment $AB$ at point $R$.

Source image reference: https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-14-052.png

Step 4: Check your work.

Measure the lengths of the two parts of line segment $AB$. If $AR$ is equal to $RB$, your construction is accurate.

record_links.rationale: This record explains that the constructed bisector is perpendicular to the original line segment.

record.evidence_quote: Take note that if you measure the angles at $R$, you will find they are $90^{\circ}$. We say that the bisector is perpendicular to the original line segment. The symbol for perpendicular is $\perp$, so we write: $PQ \perp AB$. When we do a construction to bisect a line, the bisector is always perpendicular to the line.
record.content_text:
Take note that if you measure the angles at $R$, you will find they are $90^{\circ}$. We say that the bisector is perpendicular to the original line segment. The symbol for perpendicular is $\perp$, so we write: $PQ \perp AB$.

When we do a construction to bisect a line, the bisector is always perpendicular to the line. This means we can call the bisector a "perpendicular line bisector".
